reason: Could not break the wording, and I closed the gap the verifier left. The verifier took the opening clause only from secondary books. Archive.org full-text search inside the 1961 Anderson scans themselves (lettersofbeethov0001ludw, lettersofbeethov0001beet, lettersofbeethov0001emil, letterofbeethove0001emil, bwb_C0-AFV-895) returns: that I could not bear —I will seize Fate by the throat; it shall certainly not bend and crush me completely — Oh, it would be so lovely to live a thousand lives — No indeed, I realize now. So seize (not take or grapple), shall certainly not bend and crush, and Oh, it would be so lovely are all Anderson’s, and not the older translations: the Musical Vienna 1939 text reads never overcome me and would I could have a thousand lives, and others read not wholly overcome me. The date is confirmed as Anderson no. 54, to Wegeler, 16 November 1801, by the index of the 1977 Detroit Beethoven Congress volume. shipped.js: not shipped, Beethoven at 0 of 3, not banned. It is a letter, so in scope. The source is 135 characters with no dash. Two small points, neither fatal. (1) In Anderson the sentence runs on after lives with a dash, so the closing full stop ends an excerpt, not a sentence. That is common practice and Lockwood prints it the same way, but a note should say it. (2) Adding the letter number makes the source both shorter and more locatable.
